why_how.text: The DMV checks who you are, that you may be in the country and that you live in Wisconsin before issuing a license.
Bringing valid originals the first time saves a second trip.

scenario.text: Lena brings her passport, one electric bill and a photocopy of her Social Security card.

reasoning.text: The passport covers name, birth date and status, but residence needs two documents and photocopies are refused.

result.text: Lena returns with a second residence document and her signed original Social Security card.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking one utility bill is enough to prove Wisconsin residence.

correction.text: Residence needs two documents showing your name and Wisconsin address.

prompt.text: A friend plans to prove residence with one bank statement. What is missing?

answer.text: A second document showing her name and Wisconsin address.

rationale.text: Residence always takes two documents, even though one passport can cover name, birth date and status.

narration.text: This lesson is about the paperwork that starts every Wisconsin license. The licenses in this chapter are Class D, the non-commercial license for driving a car or a light truck. You apply in person at a DMV service center, and you bring documents that prove several separate things about you. The lesson walks through each one: your name and date of birth, your citizenship or legal status, your identity, your Wisconsin residence and your Social Security number. It ends with the rule that every document must be valid, which is where many first visits go wrong.

lines.text: Apply in person at a service center.
Birth certificate or passport proves name.
The same document can prove status.

narration.text: When you apply in person, you first prove your full name and date of birth, for example with a U.S. birth certificate or a passport. You also prove U.S. citizenship or legal status, and the same birth certificate or passport can serve for that as well. That is a useful shortcut: one strong document can satisfy two requirements at once. It does not cover everything, though. Identity, residence and your Social Security number are separate items, so plan your folder of documents around the full list rather than assuming one passport handles it all.

lines.text: Identity: signed Social Security card or photo ID.

narration.text: Proof of identity can be a signed Social Security card or a state-issued photo ID card, and showing the Social Security card also satisfies the identity requirement. Residence is where people slip. You must show two documents proving Wisconsin residence, such as a utility bill or a financial statement listing your name and Wisconsin address. You must also provide your Social Security number. Gather the two address documents early, because a recent move can mean your mail is still going to an old address and you may need time to collect a second one.

lines.text: One passport: name, birth date, status.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because one birth certificate or passport can prove both your name and date of birth and your citizenship or legal status, people assume a single document covers residence too. It does not. Residence needs two separate documents that show your name and a Wisconsin address. A question might describe someone with a passport and one bill and ask what is missing. The answer is a second residence document. Remember the pattern: one document can do double duty for identity details, but your address always takes two separate proofs.

lines.text: One bank statement: enough for residence?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a friend plans to prove her Wisconsin residence with one bank statement. What is missing? Think about how many residence documents the handbook asks for. She needs a second document showing her name and Wisconsin address, such as a utility bill. Residence always takes two documents, even though a single birth certificate or passport can cover her name, birth date and status. She should also make sure both are originals and current, because photocopies and expired items will be turned away at the counter.

To wrap up: a Class D license lets you drive a car or light truck, and you apply in person at a DMV service center. Bring proof of name and birth date, proof of citizenship or legal status, proof of identity, two Wisconsin residence documents and your Social Security number. Every document must be valid, so photocopies and expired items are not accepted, and you must also meet physical and medical requirements. Next you will see the extra step for applicants under eighteen: finding an adult sponsor who signs the application and accepts responsibility.

why_how.text: A sponsor stands behind a young driver legally and financially, which is why the state asks for one.
The sponsor also keeps the teen on track by confirming school and verifying practice hours.

scenario.text: Omar, sixteen, lives with his aunt while his parents work abroad.

reasoning.text: When a teen does not live with a parent or guardian, a listed relative such as an aunt may sign as sponsor.

result.text: Omar's aunt signs the application as his sponsor.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking an older sibling of any age can sponsor a teen.

correction.text: A sibling or spouse may sponsor only if they are eighteen or older.

memory_support.text: Sponsor signs, accepts liability, stays till eighteen.

prompt.text: A seventeen-year-old brother offers to sponsor his younger sister, who lives with him. Can he?

answer.text: No. A sibling must be eighteen or older to sponsor.

rationale.text: Grandparents, aunts, uncles and foster parents have no stated age condition, but siblings and spouses must be at least eighteen.

lines.text: Under eighteen: an adult sponsor signs.

narration.text: If you are under eighteen, your license application needs one more thing: an adult sponsor. This lesson explains what a sponsor signs, what responsibility they accept, what they confirm about you, and how long sponsorship lasts. Then it covers who is allowed to sponsor, including relatives for teens who do not live with a parent, and the special cases where a minor files proof of insurance instead of having a sponsor at all. Knowing these rules helps your family decide who should sign before you visit the service center.

lines.text: Signs the application for a minor.

narration.text: An applicant under eighteen needs an adult sponsor to sign the Wisconsin Driver License Application. That signature means a lot. A sponsor accepts liability, which means being legally and financially responsible for incidents the minor causes while driving. The sponsor can also withdraw sponsorship at any time, which gives families a way to step back if a young driver is not ready. Because of that responsibility, sponsors usually take an active part in practice, and the handbook gives them specific duties beyond simply signing their name on the form.

lines.text: Teen is enrolled, not habitually truant.

narration.text: The sponsor confirms that the applicant under eighteen is enrolled in school and is not habitually truant. Later, the sponsor verifies the teen's practice driving hours, the supervised hours you will learn about in a later lesson. Sponsorship continues through the probationary phase until the driver turns eighteen, so the sponsor stays involved after the first license is issued. In other words, the sponsor is not a one-day signer but a partner through the whole teen licensing path, from the application through the limits on a new driver's license.

lines.text: Other listed relatives if not living with parents.

narration.text: A parent, step-parent or legal guardian may sponsor a teen, and so may the sponsoring parent of a foreign exchange student. When the teen does not live with a parent or legal guardian, other people may sign: a grandparent, an aunt or uncle, a foster parent, or a sibling or spouse who is eighteen or older. Notice that only the sibling or spouse comes with a stated age condition. The grandparent, aunt, uncle and foster parent options carry no age condition in the handbook, as long as the teen is not living with a parent or guardian.

lines.text: Living apart while studying or working.
Wards in care; married to a minor.

narration.text: Some applicants under eighteen file proof of insurance in place of a sponsor. That includes minors with no living parent, and those who live apart from their parents while studying full time or earning a living. Proof of insurance also replaces a sponsor for a minor who is a ward of the state, county or court placed in foster or religious welfare care, or who is married to a spouse under eighteen. These are listed situations, not a free choice. If none of them fits, the teen needs a sponsor from the list of eligible adults.

lines.text: Relatives sponsor teens living apart from parents.
Insurance replaces a sponsor in listed cases.

narration.text: Here is the trap: mixing up the two alternatives to a parent sponsor. A listed relative, such as a grandparent or aunt, may sponsor a teen who is not living with a parent or legal guardian. That is still sponsorship, with all the responsibility it carries. Proof of insurance is different: it replaces a sponsor altogether, and only in listed cases, such as a minor with no living parent. When a question describes a teen's living situation, first ask whether a listed relative can sign, and only then whether the case is one where insurance stands in for a sponsor.

Here is a quick check: a seventeen-year-old brother offers to sponsor his younger sister, who lives with him rather than with their parents. Can he sign? Think about the age condition. The answer is no. A sibling or spouse may sponsor only if they are eighteen or older. Grandparents, aunts, uncles and foster parents have no stated age condition, but siblings and spouses must be at least eighteen. Once the brother turns eighteen he could sign, or another listed relative could sponsor her now if she lives apart from a parent or legal guardian.

lines.text: Confirms school, verifies hours, until eighteen.

narration.text: In summary, an applicant under eighteen needs an adult sponsor to sign the application. The sponsor accepts legal and financial liability, can withdraw at any time, confirms school enrollment without habitual truancy, verifies practice hours and stays on until the driver turns eighteen. Parents, step-parents and guardians may sponsor; for teens not living with a parent, grandparents, aunts, uncles, foster parents and adult siblings or spouses may sign. In listed cases, proof of insurance replaces a sponsor. Next you will learn how to qualify for the instruction permit itself.

why_how.text: The instruction permit lets you practice legally with supervision before the road test.
Teens meet extra requirements so they start practice with training behind them.

scenario.text: Kai, fourteen and a half, passes the knowledge and signs tests and wants a permit today.

reasoning.text: Teens must also be at least fifteen and enrolled in driver education with its behind-the-wheel part.

result.text: Kai waits until fifteen and enrolls in driver education before applying.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking teens follow exactly the same permit path as adults.

correction.text: Teens also need to be at least fifteen and enrolled in driver education.

memory_support.text: Adults test; teens test, enroll, turn fifteen.

prompt.text: An adult of thirty has passed the knowledge test, the signs test and the vision screening. Does she also need driver education for a permit?

answer.text: No. Adults eighteen and older qualify by passing those three.

rationale.text: Driver education enrollment and the minimum age of fifteen are the extra requirements for applicants under eighteen.

narration.text: Before you can take the road test, you need practice, and in Wisconsin that practice happens on an instruction permit. This lesson explains why the permit exists and how you qualify for one. Adults and teens follow related paths, but teens have extra steps involving age and driver education, and a signed application from their driving school. Understanding these differences matters because questions often describe an applicant and ask what they still need. By the end you will be able to sort any applicant into the right path and list what remains for them.

lines.text: Pass knowledge test, signs test, vision.

narration.text: You need an instruction permit to practice driving before the road test. An applicant eighteen or older qualifies by passing three things: the knowledge test, the highway signs test and the vision screening. Those are the same first tests you learned about at the start of the handbook. Once an adult passes them, the permit allows supervised practice under companion rules you will meet in the next lesson. Notice that the adult path does not mention driver education enrollment, which is one of the clearest differences from the path for younger applicants.

An applicant under eighteen must meet the adult requirements and more. They must be at least fifteen, and enrolled in driver education, including its behind-the-wheel portion. The behind-the-wheel school gives the teen a signed copy of the Wisconsin Driver License Application, which must be completed before applying for the permit. So a teen's folder for the permit visit holds the school's signed application alongside the documents and sponsor signature from earlier lessons. Missing the school paperwork is a common reason a teen's permit visit has to be rescheduled.

lines.text: Driving school also supplies a signed one.

narration.text: Here is a bridge between this lesson and the last. The same application form number shows up twice in the teen path. First, a sponsor signs the Wisconsin Driver License Application for an applicant under eighteen. Second, the behind-the-wheel school also supplies a signed copy of that application. Both signatures are part of getting a teen started. If a question mentions the application and asks who signs it, remember that the sponsor signs to accept responsibility, while the driving school signs as part of driver education, before the teen applies for the permit.

lines.text: Adult passed all three tests: driver ed too?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: an adult of thirty has passed the knowledge test, the highway signs test and the vision screening. Does she also need driver education to get an instruction permit? Work through the two paths. The answer is no. Adults eighteen and older qualify by passing those three items. Driver education enrollment, with its behind-the-wheel portion, and a minimum age of fifteen are the extra requirements for applicants under eighteen. Her next step is supervised practice with a qualified companion, which is the subject of the next lesson.

lines.text: Teens: tests plus age and driver ed.

narration.text: To wrap up: an instruction permit lets you practice before the road test. An adult eighteen or older qualifies by passing the knowledge test, the highway signs test and the vision screening. An applicant under eighteen must also be at least fifteen and enrolled in driver education, including behind-the-wheel training, and the driving school supplies a signed application that must be completed before applying. With the permit in hand, the next question is who may ride with you, and the handbook's companion rules are some of the most detailed in this chapter.

why_how.text: A permit driver is still learning, so an experienced, licensed adult must always be there to help.
The age and seating rules decide exactly who may ride along and when.

scenario.text: Tess, sixteen with a permit, wants to drive at night with her twenty-two-year-old cousin beside her.

reasoning.text: Darkness driving needs a qualified instructor or a licensed person aged twenty-five beside her.

result.text: Tess drives at night only with an instructor or a qualified twenty-five-year-old beside her.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any licensed adult can supervise a permit driver.

correction.text: The companion needs two years of experience on a valid regular license, not a probationary or occupational one.

memory_support.text: Family nineteen, anyone else twenty-one, dark twenty-five.

prompt.text: A twenty-year-old family friend with a regular license wants to supervise a permit driver. What stops him?

answer.text: He is under twenty-one and is not an instructor, parent, guardian or spouse.

rationale.text: Only instructors and parents, guardians or spouses may be nineteen; anyone else must be at least twenty-one.

title.text: Who rides with a permit driver

narration.text: A permit lets you practice, but never on your own. This lesson covers the companion rules in detail: what license and experience the companion needs, how old different companions must be, where they sit, when family may ride in the back, when written permission is required, who else may ride along, and the stricter rule for driving in darkness. These rules are full of similar-looking ages, nineteen, twenty-one and twenty-five, so the lesson keeps pointing out which age goes with which situation. Treat it as a checklist to run before every practice drive.

lines.text: Never drive alone on a permit.

narration.text: A Class D permit holder may never drive alone. The companion must have at least two years of licensed driving experience and a valid regular license. A probationary or occupational license does not qualify, even if the person has been driving for a while. This rule surprises people because they assume any licensed adult can supervise. The handbook is stricter: the license must be a regular one, and the experience must be at least two years. Before a practice drive, check both the companion's license type and how long they have held a license.

lines.text: Instructor or family: nineteen or older.

narration.text: The companion sits in the front passenger seat. A qualified instructor aged nineteen or older may be the companion, as may a parent, guardian or spouse aged nineteen or older, or any person aged twenty-one or older. When a parent, guardian or spouse is the companion, immediate family members of the permit holder may also ride in the back seat. And if the permit holder is under eighteen, a companion aged twenty-one or older needs written permission from the minor's parent or guardian before the drive begins, so a family friend cannot simply hop in.

lines.text: Darkness: instructor or twenty-five beside you.

narration.text: A permit holder aged at least sixteen may carry one more licensed person, aged twenty-five or older with at least two years of driving experience, in a seat other than the front seat. Driving in darkness has its own rule. It requires either a qualified instructor or a licensed person aged twenty-five with at least two years of licensed experience in the seat beside you. So the age of twenty-five appears twice: once for the extra rider behind you and once for the darkness companion beside you. The seat is what separates the two rules.

Here is the trap: three ages that are easy to swap. A front-seat companion may be nineteen only if they are a qualified instructor or a parent, guardian or spouse. Any other companion must be at least twenty-one. The extra licensed passenger allowed on a permit must be at least twenty-five, whereas the front-seat companion can be as young as nineteen. And for darkness, the person beside you must be an instructor or a licensed person aged twenty-five. When a question gives an age, ask two things: who is this person to the driver, and where are they sitting.

Here is a quick check: a twenty-year-old family friend with a regular license wants to supervise a permit driver. What stops him? Run the companion checklist. He is under twenty-one, and he is not a qualified instructor, parent, guardian or spouse, so the nineteen-year-old allowance does not apply to him. Only instructors and parents, guardians or spouses may be nineteen; anyone else must be at least twenty-one. Even after he turns twenty-one, he would need two years on a regular license and written permission from a parent if the driver is a minor.

lines.text: Regular license, two years, never alone.
Nineteen, twenty-one or twenty-five by role.

narration.text: Let us wrap up the companion rules. A permit driver never drives alone, and the companion needs a valid regular license with at least two years of experience. The companion sits in front: an instructor, parent, guardian or spouse aged nineteen or older, or anyone aged twenty-one or older, who needs written parent permission if the driver is a minor. Family may ride in back with a parent, guardian or spouse companion. One extra licensed rider aged twenty-five may sit behind, and darkness driving needs an instructor or a twenty-five-year-old beside you.

why_how.text: The probationary license marks your first solo driving, so the state wants proof of enough practice first.
Logged, verified hours, including darkness, build the experience new drivers lack.

scenario.text: Noah turns sixteen after seven months on his permit with forty-eight daytime practice hours.

reasoning.text: He needs fifty hours including ten in darkness, plus proof of driver education.

result.text: Noah adds darkness hours until the total reaches fifty, then applies with his sponsor's verification.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a sixteenth birthday is enough to get a probationary license.

correction.text: A teen also needs six months on the permit and proof of driver education.

memory_support.text: Six months, sixteen, fifty hours, ten dark.

prompt.text: A teen has driven fifty supervised hours, all in daylight. What still blocks the probationary license?

answer.text: Ten of the hours must be in darkness.

rationale.text: The total is forty daytime plus ten darkness hours, so daylight driving alone cannot complete it.

narration.text: This lesson covers the step from permit to your first license, the probationary license. You will learn when it is issued and how old you must be, the strict rule about phones, what an applicant under eighteen must complete first, and the supervised practice hours that have to be logged and verified. The practice rules include a specific number of hours in darkness, which people often forget. By the end you should be able to look at any teen's progress and say exactly what is still missing before they can apply. Take each requirement one at a time.

lines.text: First license after the skills test.

narration.text: The probationary license is the first license issued after you pass the skills test, and you must be at least sixteen to receive it. It comes with an important rule: phones may not be used while driving on a probationary license except to report an emergency. That means no calls, no texting and no casual phone use behind the wheel. Holding this license is real independence, but the phone rule and the graduated limits in the next lesson show that the state still treats you as a new driver who needs fewer distractions.

An applicant under eighteen must hold the instruction permit for at least six months, be sixteen, and prove completion of driver education before getting the probationary license. All three are required together. A teen who turns sixteen after only a few months on a permit is not yet eligible, and neither is a teen who has held the permit for a year but has not finished driver education. Think of the requirements as three boxes that must all be ticked, with the sponsor helping to keep track along the way. Plan the three together from the start.

Supervised practice on the permit must total at least fifty hours, made up of forty daytime hours and ten hours in darkness, with a qualified adult. Fifty hours is only the minimum, and more may be needed to show safe driving. The sponsor must verify the full fifty hours, including the ten after dark. To keep track, sponsors can print a driving log or use the RoadReady mobile app. Logging each drive as it happens is far easier than trying to reconstruct months of practice from memory just before the application. Steady logging pays off at application time.

Here is the trap. A teen who logs fifty hours, all in daylight, has met the total but not the rule. Permit practice needs forty daytime hours and ten darkness hours, so the fifty-hour total cannot be met with daytime driving alone. Darkness driving also has its own companion rule from the previous lesson: an instructor or a licensed person aged twenty-five beside you. Plan night drives deliberately, especially in summer when it stays light late, so the darkness hours do not become a last-minute scramble before the application.

Here is a quick check: a teen has driven fifty supervised hours, all in daylight. What still blocks the probationary license? Look at how the hours are split. Ten of the hours must be in darkness. The rule is forty daytime hours plus ten darkness hours, so daylight driving alone cannot complete it. The teen also needs six months on the permit, a sixteenth birthday and proof of driver education, and the sponsor must verify the full total. Adding night drives with a qualified companion fixes the hours, and the rest is paperwork.

To sum up: the probationary license is the first license after the skills test, issued at sixteen or older, and phones may be used while driving only to report an emergency. An applicant under eighteen needs six months on the permit, age sixteen and proof of driver education. Supervised practice must total at least fifty hours, forty in daytime and ten in darkness, verified by the sponsor and tracked with a printed log or the RoadReady app. Next you will learn the graduated limits that apply during the first months of that probationary license.

why_how.text: The graduated limits cut distractions for new drivers under eighteen during their riskiest months.
The rules change with the hour, so knowing the two windows keeps every trip legal.

scenario.text: Ava, sixteen and three months into her GDL, wants to drive two friends to a movie ending at eleven at night.

reasoning.text: In the daytime window she may carry one other passenger plus one qualifying licensed adult, not two friends.

result.text: Ava takes one friend, or adds a qualifying licensed adult to the trip.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the passenger limit only applies after midnight.

correction.text: The same one-plus-one limit for non-family riders applies in both windows.

prompt.text: At one in the morning, a GDL driver wants to drive alone to a friend's house. Is that allowed?

answer.text: No. Between midnight and five a.m. driving alone is allowed only between home, school and work.

rationale.text: The daytime window allows driving alone anywhere; the midnight window limits solo trips to home, school and work.

narration.text: Your probationary license comes with limits designed to keep new drivers safe. This lesson explains the graduated driver license, often shortened to GDL: why the limits exist, how long they last, and exactly what they allow during the day and late at night. You will learn the passenger rules for family and for everyone else, what makes the limits last longer, what happens with points, and when the limits end for good. Because the rules depend on the time of day, the lesson treats the daytime and midnight windows separately and then compares them directly.

lines.text: Another name for the probationary license.

narration.text: The probationary license is also called a graduated driver license, or GDL, and its passenger and hour limits apply to drivers under eighteen to cut distractions. The limits last for the first nine months unless the driver turns eighteen sooner, and no new license is needed when they end. The idea is simple: fewer passengers and less late-night driving during the months when new drivers are most likely to be distracted. Once the period is over, the same license simply carries on without the limits, so there is no extra trip to the service center.

Between five in the morning and midnight, a GDL driver may drive alone anywhere and may carry any number of immediate family members. A GDL driver may also carry one other passenger plus one licensed adult with at least two years of experience who is a qualified instructor or spouse aged nineteen or older, or anyone aged twenty-one or older. So family riders are unlimited in this window, while everyone else is limited to that one-plus-one combination. Two friends with no qualifying adult would be one passenger too many.

lines.text: Alone only for home, school, work.

narration.text: Between midnight and five in the morning, a GDL driver may drive alone only when traveling between home, school and work. During those hours the same passenger limit applies: one qualifying licensed adult with at least two years of experience plus one other person. So the difference between the windows is mostly about where you may drive alone. In the daytime window you may go anywhere; after midnight a solo trip must connect home, school and work. A late shift ending after midnight is allowed, but a solo drive to a friend's house is not.

Here is the trap. People remember that the night window is stricter and assume every rule changes at midnight. Only the driving-alone rule changes. In the five a.m. to midnight window a GDL driver may go anywhere alone, but in the midnight to five a.m. window driving alone is allowed only between home, school and work. The passenger limit for non-family riders, one qualifying licensed adult plus one other person, is the same in both windows. So a question about passengers at ten at night and at two in the morning has the same answer.

lines.text: Violation or breach adds six months.

narration.text: The GDL limits are extended by six months after a moving violation conviction, any breach of the limits, or a suspension or revocation for any reason. So the normal nine months can become fifteen. The handbook also says points on second or later convictions double during this phase, as with the permit, and enough points on your record can cost you the license. Finally, the GDL hour and passenger limits stop applying once the driver turns eighteen, whichever comes first. Driving carefully is the fastest way through this phase.

lines.text: One a.m. solo drive to a friend?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: at one in the morning, a GDL driver wants to drive alone to a friend's house. Is that allowed? Decide which window applies first. The answer is no. Between midnight and five a.m. driving alone is allowed only between home, school and work. The daytime window, from five a.m. to midnight, allows driving alone anywhere, but that window has closed. If the driver breaks the limit anyway, the limits are extended by six months, so the late trip would cost far more than it is worth. Patience now saves months later.

lines.text: Nine months, plus six for breaches.
Day anywhere; night home, school, work.

narration.text: To finish: the GDL limits apply to drivers under eighteen for the first nine months. From five a.m. to midnight you may drive alone anywhere with unlimited family riders and one other passenger plus one qualifying adult. From midnight to five a.m. you may drive alone only between home, school and work, with the same passenger limit. A moving violation, a breach or a suspension adds six months, later conviction points double, and the limits end at eighteen. Next you will learn about the regular license, transfers from other states and REAL ID.

why_how.text: The regular license is the last step, and it needs renewing on a fixed schedule.
Newcomers face transfer deadlines that differ for regular and commercial licenses, and REAL ID documents must be shown again.

scenario.text: Rosa moves to Wisconsin with a regular license from another state and a REAL ID from there.

reasoning.text: She has sixty days to apply, and her old REAL ID does not carry over, so she brings all documents again.

result.text: Rosa applies within sixty days with a full set of REAL ID documents.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a REAL ID from another state transfers to Wisconsin automatically.

correction.text: A REAL ID does not carry over; you present all acceptable documents again.

memory_support.text: Sixty regular, thirty commercial; star means REAL.

prompt.text: A truck driver with a commercial license moves to Wisconsin. How long does he have to apply for a Wisconsin CDL?

rationale.text: Commercial license holders have thirty days, while regular license holders have sixty.

narration.text: This final lesson of the chapter looks past the probationary phase. You will learn how the regular driver license follows the probationary one, how often it must be renewed and when you may renew early, and when the reminder arrives. Then the lesson turns to people moving to Wisconsin from another state, who face deadlines that depend on the kind of license they hold. It ends with REAL ID: what it is, how Wisconsin marks it, why an old one does not carry over, and when you need it to travel or enter federal buildings.

title.text: Renewing to and as a regular

lines.text: Renew ninety days before it expires.

narration.text: The regular driver license is the final step after the probationary license, and renewal can begin ninety days before the probationary license expires. After that, a regular license must be renewed every eight years. Renewal is allowed up to one year ahead of expiration, and it can be done online or at a service center. A renewal reminder arrives forty-five to sixty days before your birthday in the year your license expires. Even so, do not rely only on the reminder; know the year your license expires so a lost letter does not leave you driving on an expired license.

lines.text: Probationary to regular: ninety days early.
Regular renewal: up to one year early.

narration.text: Here is the trap: two early-renewal windows with different lengths. Moving from a probationary license to a regular one can begin ninety days before the probationary license expires. Renewing a regular license, which happens every eight years, may be done up to one year early. And the reminder letter is a third number, arriving forty-five to sixty days before your birthday in the expiration year. When a question asks how early you may renew, first decide which license is being renewed, because the answer is ninety days for one and up to a year for the other.

lines.text: Regular license: apply within sixty days.

narration.text: A new resident holding another state's regular license is an out-of-state transfer and should apply for a Wisconsin license within sixty days of moving. A commercial driver license holder from another state should apply for the Wisconsin CDL within thirty days of moving. So the commercial deadline is half as long as the regular one. If you are moving with a commercial license, put the thirty-day date on your calendar as soon as you arrive, because the shorter deadline is the one most likely to slip past during a busy relocation.

lines.text: Does not carry over from another state.

narration.text: A REAL ID meets U.S. Department of Homeland Security standards, and Wisconsin marks its REAL ID cards with a star. A REAL ID from your previous state does not carry over, so you must present all acceptable documents again to get a Wisconsin REAL ID. Beginning May seventh, two thousand twenty-five, flying within the U.S. or entering a military base or other federal building requires REAL ID-compliant identification or another accepted ID such as a passport. If you have a passport, it is an accepted alternative for those trips.

Here is a quick check: a truck driver with a commercial license moves to Wisconsin. How long does he have to apply for a Wisconsin CDL? Recall the two transfer deadlines. The answer is thirty days from moving. Commercial license holders have thirty days, while regular license holders have sixty. If he also wants a Wisconsin REAL ID, he will need to bring all acceptable documents again, because a REAL ID from his old state does not carry over. A star on his new card would show that it meets federal standards. Write the date down on arrival.

lines.text: Sixty or thirty days to transfer.

narration.text: To close the chapter: the regular license follows the probationary license, with renewal beginning ninety days before the probationary license expires, then every eight years, up to one year early, online or at a service center, with a reminder forty-five to sixty days before your birthday. New residents have sixty days to transfer a regular license and thirty for a commercial one. A REAL ID is marked with a star, does not carry over from another state, and is needed, or a passport, for domestic flights, military bases and federal buildings.
